pages.blurb: Opened in September 1993; Bryan Gee's Movement made it drum & bass's weekly, still running fortnightly at the 2008 relaunch.

pages.blurb: High Street bar of about 250 where Sgt Pokes and Loefah worked, home of the Dub Sessions and Croydub nights.

pages.blurb: A Nazi air-raid shelter given over to hardcore and gabber, now the Boros collection.

pages.blurb: The Camden theatre, now KOKO, where Colin Faver and Eddie Richards played electro, funk, then early acid to London; Mr. C rapped in Richards's Jolly Roger act.

pages.name: Eden
pages.blurb: San Antonio; Judge Jules's Judgement Sundays.

pages.blurb: Open-air museum of five lignite-mining machines on the Gremminer See, framing a 25,000-capacity arena; Melt's home from 1999 to 2024.

pages.name: Front
pages.blurb: Willi Prange and Phillip Clarke's gay club, with Klaus Stockhausen; one of the first house clubs in continental Europe.

pages.name: Gatecrasher
pages.blurb: The Republic; the "Gatecrasher kids" with their cyber-hair; the home of trance.

pages.blurb: Factory People's Beirut club, damaged in the 2020 port explosion and reopened in 2023.

pages.blurb: Leather and dress-code club in the Vauxhall arches that closed in December 2016 after 21 years.

pages.name: Lost

pages.blurb: Twitch and Brainstorm; Mills and Clarke as regulars.

pages.name: Rex Club
pages.blurb: Under the Grand Rex; Garnier's Wake Up.

pages.name: Shoom
pages.blurb: A Southwark fitness centre on Saturday nights; Danny and Jenni Rampling; 300 people who opened everything else.

pages.name: Speed
pages.blurb: The Mars Bar, Covent Garden; Bukem and Fabio's Thursday of atmospheric drum & bass.

pages.blurb: David Mancuso's invitation-only parties; the root of the Garage.

pages.name: The Rocket
pages.blurb: Holloway Road venue that housed Megadog's monthly all-nighter and a Return to the Source residency.

pages.name: Trade
pages.blurb: Turnmills, Sunday mornings; Tony De Vit; the gay after-hours that became hard house.

pages.name: Twilo
pages.blurb: Sasha and Digweed's monthly; the Phazon sound system.

pages.name: Vague
pages.blurb: Leeds night from Suzy Mason and Paul Fryer, at the Warehouse, billed as mixed; Pete Tong recorded an Essential Mix there.

pages.name: Block9
pages.blurb: Gideon Berger and Stephen Gallagher's design company, makers of the NYC Downlow, the London Underground, Genosys and IICON at Glastonbury.

pages.blurb: Lisbon group named for Buraca, who took kuduro to clubs worldwide with M.I.A. and founded Enchufada; reunited in 2026.

pages.name: DIMS (Drug Information and Monitoring System)
pages.blurb: Dutch drug-testing network of 32 addiction-care organisations, coordinated by the Trimbos Institute, which issues national Red Alerts.

pages.name: Exodus Collective
pages.blurb: Luton's free-party and housing collective; the political wing of the sound systems.

pages.name: Hastings Techno Militia
pages.blurb: The Hastings residents — DJK, Japhy, Rob Miller — who took the Detroit crew's name after hosting them: a vinyl crew playing Detroit techno in a Sussex seaside town, promoting nights at the Brewing Brothers Courtyard and sending DJK to play Detroit and bring the new wax home.

pages.name: Insomniac
pages.blurb: Pasquale Rotella's Los Angeles promoter behind EDC, Nocturnal Wonderland and Electric Forest; in partnership with Live Nation from 2013.

pages.name: Lifeline (Manchester)
pages.blurb: Drugs charity whose Peanut Pete and Claire and Jose comics took harm-reduction advice to ravers in the early 1990s.

pages.name: Mamba Negra
pages.blurb: Party collective founded in May 2013 by Cashu and Laura Diaz, staging nights in abandoned buildings across São Paulo.

pages.name: Mutoid Waste Company
pages.blurb: Post-apocalyptic sculpture from scrap, mobile sound systems and Spiral Tribe's collaborators; Glastonbury's Trash City descends from them.

pages.name: Paxahau
pages.blurb: Detroit rave producer founded by Jason Huvaere; took over Movement at Hart Plaza in 2006.

pages.blurb: Festival group founded with Providence money in 2017 and led by James Barton; bought by KKR in 2024, with CVC investing alongside.

pages.blurb: Code-word scheme devised by Hayley Crawford at Lincolnshire County Council in 2016 and adopted by venues across Britain.

pages.name: Batty Bass

pages.name: Big Beach Boutique II

pages.name: Black & Blue
pages.blurb: Montreal's AIDS benefit circuit festival, begun in 1991 with about 800 people and peaking at 17,000 in 1999.

pages.name: Boiler Room
pages.blurb: A webcam in a Hackney boiler room; the format of the decade.

pages.blurb: Graham Bright's bill: £20,000 fines and six months for unlicensed parties.

pages.name: Cocktail d'Amore

pages.name: Dekmantel
pages.blurb: The Amsterdamse Bos; the taste-maker's line-up.

pages.name: DMZ
pages.blurb: Mala, Coki, Loefah and Sgt Pokes's night in Third Base and Mass, the club in St Matthew's Church, Brixton.

pages.name: Dubmission
pages.blurb: E-Werk's Saturday house-and-trance night, where Paul van Dyk was resident and out of which came his 'For an Angel'.

pages.name: Electric Daisy Carnival UK
pages.blurb: Insomniac and Cream's British EDC at the National Bowl in Milton Keynes; over 50,000 at the first, by Insomniac's count.

pages.name: Energy
pages.blurb: Jeremy Taylor and Karl Jewell; Membury airfield; the convoys.

pages.name: Fuji Rock Festival

pages.name: HARD Summer
pages.blurb: Gary Richards's Los Angeles festival; Live Nation took a majority stake in 2012; two deaths on the first day of the 2015 Pomona edition were followed by county case-by-case review of large events.

pages.name: Homelands Ireland
pages.blurb: Mean Fiddler and Irish promoters' festival at a former Butlins resort in County Meath, 25 September 1999; Orbital and Underworld headlined.

pages.name: Jungle Fever
pages.blurb: The rave brand that grew out of Kool FM in 1993, a home for ragga jungle's DJs and MCs.
